runs.text: There are 6 FPGs in Tukangbesi of Sulawesi, Indonesia. The Wolio people are one of them.

The Wolio people (also known as Baubau, Buton, or Butung) inhabit the small islands of Buton, Muna, and Kabaena in Southeast Sulawesi. They are descendants of 15th-century immigrants from Johor, Malaysia, who established the Buton Dynasty. In 1540, the sixth king converted to Islam, transforming the kingdom into a sultanate that lasted until 1960. Today, Buton is known for its asphalt production and is being explored for oil and mineral resources. Many Wolio have migrated to other regions like Maluku and Papua in search of work. They speak the Wolio language, and some also understand Arabic, which is used in religious and historical texts.

In Wolio villages, markets sell cloth materials like silk and cotton, and small shops and peddlers are common. The Wolio people farm both land and sea—growing rice, corn, and cassava, and cultivating seaweed (agar-agar) from June to September. Many also work as sailors and shipbuilders, taking advantage of the rich marine life around Buton and Muna. Their traditional houses are elevated, made of boards, with roofs of wooden planks or coconut leaves; men work outside while women manage the home and finances. Baubau has become an official city, creating development opportunities; the Wolio people highly value education and language learning, leading to social advancement.
Almost all Wolio have beliefs centered in Sufi Islam. According to their teachings, they practice
meditation to receive visions from God, or to find hidden truths

The Wolio need greater opportunities for work that can provide enough money for their livelihood. Because of the Wolio people’s geographical situation, along a major sea lane through Indonesia, there is a great deal of tourism potential for the city. Their fishermen need better training and more knowledge to improve production and distribution of their sea products. In addition, teachers and educators are needed to satisfy the Wolio people’s thirst for knowledge and to develop their potential.

Pray for open hearts among the Wolio people to encounter the love, grace, and freedom found in Jesus Christ, despite cultural and religious barriers.
Pray for missionaries, educators, and local believers who can humbly and wisely share the gospel in culturally sensitive and respectful ways.
Pray for the city of Baubau, that its growth and development would bring blessings and not spiritual distraction, and that it would become a place of light and truth.
Pray for healing from historical wounds, especially those related to colonialism, cultural loss, and identity, so that Wolio people may know that their true identity is found in Christ.
